headline: Zscaler grows revenue 20% with record free cash flow, and agrees to be acquired by CrowdStrike
takeaway: Revenue rose 20% to $949 million and annual recurring revenue 21% to $3.88 billion, with record operating cash flow of $541 million. On the same day Zscaler agreed to be acquired by CrowdStrike for about $43.9 billion in stock, and its shares jumped 17.7%.
results: Revenue grew 20% to $949.3 million and ARR 21% to $3.88 billion. Net new ARR was $111 million; excluding the contribution from the Red Canary acquisition a year earlier, it grew 22%. Non-GAAP gross margin improved to 80.8% from 79.9%.

Zscaler remained loss-making on a GAAP basis, with a net loss of $27.4 million ($0.17 per share) against $11.6 million a year earlier, mainly because of stock compensation. Non-GAAP operating income rose to $230.2 million, a 24.3% margin, and non-GAAP earnings per share to $1.23 from $0.96. Operating cash flow was a record $541 million and free cash flow a record $416.5 million.
mgmt: Chief executive Jay Chaudhry said AI is driving the biggest security transformation of his lifetime because attackers can now automate exploits at unprecedented speed, and that Zscaler’s zero-trust architecture becomes non-negotiable as companies deploy AI agents.

He said the combination with CrowdStrike would create the most expansive cybersecurity platform for the AI era, covering cloud, network and endpoint. Zscaler shareholders will receive 1.135 CrowdStrike shares for each Zscaler share.
view: The quarter was solid but not spectacular: 20% growth is healthy for a company of this size, though it trails CrowdStrike’s accelerating growth, and free cash flow margin fell from 52% to 44% of revenue. Those numbers help explain why Zscaler accepted an offer: as a standalone company it was growing more slowly than its peers and its shares had underperformed.

With the deal, Zscaler shares now trade on CrowdStrike’s price and the odds of the deal closing. At $231.62 on November 24 the shares sat close to the value of 1.135 CrowdStrike shares, which means the market expects the deal to go through and attaches little extra risk to it.

For Zscaler holders, the investment case has become CrowdStrike’s case. Anyone who wants to own Zscaler today should be comfortable owning CrowdStrike at about 136 times forward earnings, because that is what they will receive. If regulators block the deal, the shares would likely fall back toward their previous level.
watch: Regulatory and shareholder approval of the CrowdStrike deal, and the spread between Zscaler’s price and the value of the exchange ratio.
